subject: biology-hl
topicLabel: D2.3 — Water potential & A2.1 — Origin of cells (Jan unit)

items.stem: Water potential (Ψ) is measured in and has its maximum value at:
items.note: Ψ in kilopascals; pure water has the maximum possible water potential, defined as 0 kPa. All solutions have negative Ψ.

items.stem: Adding solute to pure water changes the water potential by:
choices: No change — only pressure changes Ψ
items.note: Solute potential (Ψs) is always negative and becomes more negative with more dissolved solute — water is 'held' by the solute.
Ψw = Ψs + Ψp: solute potential + pressure potential. In an open beaker Ψp = 0, so Ψw = Ψs.
Water moves down the water-potential gradient: from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) Ψ — i.e. toward the more concentrated solution.

items.stem: A turgid plant cell has a pressure potential that is:
choices: Positive — the wall pushes back on the contents
items.note: As water enters, the protoplast presses on the cell wall → positive Ψp raises Ψw until net movement stops (turgor). Plasmolysed cells have Ψp ≈ 0.

items.stem: A red blood cell is placed in pure water. It will:
choices: Swell and potentially burst (lyse) — no cell wall
items.note: Pure water (Ψ = 0) vs cell interior (negative Ψ) → water floods in. Animal cells lack a wall → they lyse; plant cells become turgid instead.

items.stem: Osmolarity is measured with an osmometer, which works by:
choices: Measuring the freezing point depression of the sample
items.note: More solute particles lower the freezing point — osmometers convert freezing-point depression into osmolality (mol/kg).

items.stem: Salting meat or preserving fruit in concentrated sugar syrup prevents microbial growth because:
choices: Salt and sugar are toxic to all bacteria
The high external solute concentration lowers Ψ → water leaves microbial cells
items.note: High external solute → very negative Ψ outside → microbes lose water by osmosis. A real-world application of water potential.

items.stem: A plant cell with Ψs = −500 kPa and Ψp = +200 kPa is placed in a solution with Ψw = −450 kPa. Water will:
items.note: Cell Ψw = −500 + 200 = −300 kPa. Solution Ψw = −450 kPa. Water moves from higher (−300) to lower (−450) → out → plasmolysis.

items.stem: An isotonic solution for animal cells means:
choices: Same solute concentration as the cell interior — no net water movement
Higher solute concentration than the cell
items.note: Isotonic = equal osmolarity → no net osmosis. Hypertonic → cells shrink; hypotonic → cells swell/lyse.

items.stem: Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment provided evidence that:
choices: Cells arise only from pre-existing cells
The first cells came from space
items.note: Sterile broth stayed sterile unless the curved neck let dust in — life did not appear spontaneously. This creates the origins paradox the cell theory can't explain directly.

choices: Amino acids can form abiotically from inorganic gases and electrical sparks
items.note: Sparks through a reducing atmosphere (H₂, CH₄, NH₃, H₂O) produced amino acids — evidence that early Earth conditions could build organic monomers.

items.stem: Which is NOT evidence supporting the endosymbiotic theory for mitochondria?
choices: They have their own circular DNA
They have a linear nucleus-like genome
items.note: Mitochondria/chloroplasts: double membrane, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, similar size to bacteria, binary fission — engulfed prokaryote ancestors.

items.stem: The last universal common ancestor (LUCA) is inferred from:
choices: Shared genes and biochemistry across all life (DNA code, ATP, universal genetic code)
items.note: All life shares the same genetic code, ATP and ribosome machinery — the simplest explanation is descent from one common ancestor.

items.stem: Extremophiles (e.g. heat-loving bacteria near hydrothermal vents) are relevant to cell origins because they:
choices: Show cells can survive in conditions thought to resemble early Earth
items.note: Life thriving at high temperature/pressure/acidity supports the idea that the first cells tolerated harsh early-Earth conditions.

items.stem: Which sequence correctly orders stages in the origin of cells?
choices: Abiotic synthesis of monomers → polymers → self-replicating molecules → membranes enclosing them → cells
items.note: Standard outline: abiotic monomers (Miller–Urey) → polymers → self-replicating molecules (RNA-era discussion) → compartmentalizing membranes → first cells.

items.stem: A plant cell has a solute potential of −500 kPa and a pressure potential of +200 kPa. Calculate its water potential, and predict and explain what happens when it is placed in pure water.
markscheme: Pure water Ψw = 0 kPa — higher than the cell (1)
Water enters the cell down the gradient (1)
Cell becomes turgid: Ψp rises until cell Ψw reaches 0 and net movement stops (1)
items.tactic: Water-potential calculations: write the equation, quote the value, then give the direction with the reason. Pure water = 0 anchors every comparison.

items.stem: Evaluate the evidence for the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts.
markscheme: Structural evidence: double membrane consistent with engulfment + vesicle enclosure (1)
Own circular DNA like bacteria, and 70S ribosomes, binary fission (1)
Size comparable to free-living bacteria; genetic code shared with host (1)
Limitation: the events occurred ~1.5+ billion years ago — they cannot be directly observed; the conclusion is an inference from multiple converging lines of evidence (1)
items.tactic: 'Evaluate' answers need the supporting evidence AND the limitation. Name at least two structural similarities plus the inference caveat.
